newsitem.title: UK: LME ZINC PREMIUM UP BY 50 PCT AS SQUEEZE HURTS.
newsitem.headline: LME ZINC PREMIUM UP BY 50 PCT AS SQUEEZE HURTS.

text.p: Tightness in zinc hit the premium for cash metal, which zoomed up by more than 50 percent on Friday, and the spread in aluminium also held at strong levels.
The movements occurred despite a warning by the LME on Thursday about players with dominant positions pushing prices higher.
The strength of the spreads helped to stabilise three months prices, which had corrected lower in the morning from heady levels the previous evening.
In zinc, players scrambled in the afternoon ring and bid up the cash/threes spread, which ballooned to a $155 backwardation from $100 on Thursday.

One trader said it appeared to be a liquidity problem after cash metal was bid up during the morning but another said renewed rumours of personnel changes in the Chinese metals industry may have triggered speculative moves.
An official at China's Zhuzhou zinc smelter on Tuesday denied rumours of sackings following big losses on global metals markets.
Chinese smelters last year sold forward at low prices as much as 250,000 tonnes, and most of the positions mature in September.
On the LME on Friday, the bulk of the tightness was in the September/August spread, at a $90 backwardation.
Three months zinc took a back seat, ending $7 firmer at $1,547.
Aluminium found renewed buying interest after correcting lower in the morning to a low of $1,732.
"I think the market needed that.., it confirmed support down there," said analyst Robin Bahr of broker Brandeis.
Three months ended the day with pared losses at $1,746, down $16.50.
Next week should see more of the same, said Bahr. "Any weakness will be taken as an opportunity to establish or re-establish long positions," he said.
Tightness kept bubbling under the market, with the cash/threes ending at a $15/$20 backwardation, little changed from Thursday's $20.
Copper slipped in the afternoon after fund selling on Comex triggered stops, hitting a low of $2,284.
But the market found good base support and stabilised, ending the day $45 lower at $2,288.
A stocks increase of 2,925 tonnes reminded the market of rising inventories and a looming surplus.
Speculative selling on nickel forced prices to a low of $7,010, a long-term support level, but prices edged higher by the close to end $175 softer at $7,085.
"Once nickel starts slipping, the momentum can take it lower...If the specs keep hunting for stops, they might trigger some under $7,000," Bahr said.
Lead dipped $4 to $614 while tin dipped $30 to $5,605.
Alloy ended little changed at $1,545/47.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542-8065
